opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very healthy sign, honestly. When OpenClaw came out, what it showed everyone was that the model had quietly crossed a threshold. It wasn't just chatting anymore. It could actually operate: open a terminal, call tools, keep a task alive for hours, recover from its own mistakes. Once people saw that, it was natural for many teams in China to move quickly and build their own versions.

I'd split the products into a few layers. The first wave is mostly about packaging: making it easy to install, connecting it to local apps like WeChat, Feishu and DingTalk, and handling deployment and cloud hosting. That's real value. Most ordinary users will never set up an open-source agent on a Mac mini themselves, so lowering that barrier matters a lot. But at that layer the moat is thin, because everyone is wrapping roughly the same capability.

The more interesting question is what sits underneath. An agent like this is really a stress test for the base model. Long-horizon tasks expose everything: whether the model can keep context over dozens or hundreds of steps, whether its tool calls are reliable, whether it knows when it's stuck, and the cost per task. A demo that works once is easy. Running every day for real users at an acceptable token cost is very hard. So I look less at the shell and more at whether the team owns, or deeply optimizes, the model doing the work.

From my side, as someone building models, this changes what we optimize for. A few years ago the race was benchmark scores on single-turn reasoning. Now the important things are agentic: efficiency over long contexts, stable tool use, inference cost, and how the model behaves in a messy real environment rather than a clean eval. Chinese teams are actually well positioned here, because we've had to be very disciplined about efficiency, through architecture, training recipes, and inference optimization. When an agent burns millions of tokens on one task, efficiency stops being a technical detail and becomes the product.

There are also real concerns. Security is the big one. Giving an agent access to your files, accounts and messages is a huge trust decision, and prompt injection is far from solved. I'd like the industry to treat permissions, sandboxing and auditability as first-class features rather than afterthoughts, before a serious incident forces the issue.

So overall, I'm positive. The fast follow is fine, that's how ecosystems form. But the teams that last will be the ones that use this moment to push the model capability itself, not just ride the hype around the interface.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the speed itself is the signal. When OpenClaw took off, within a few weeks you had maybe a dozen Chinese teams shipping something that looked structurally similar: a local agent that can actually touch your files, your browser, your terminal, and chain actions together without you babysitting each step. That reflex, where a new paradigm appears and the ecosystem converges on it almost instantly, is something China's product culture is genuinely good at. But I'd separate the question into three layers, because "like OpenClaw" is doing a lot of work in that phrase.

The first layer is the shell, the product form. Most of what launched is honestly quite close to the original: the harness, the tool-calling loop, the permission model, the way it surfaces what it's doing. Some teams did meaningful localization work, like deep integration with WeChat, Feishu, DingTalk, domestic cloud storage, payment flows. That matters more than it sounds, because an agent is only as useful as the surfaces it can reach, and in China those surfaces are different. So on this layer I'd say the adaptation is real, but it's adaptation, not invention.

The second layer is the model underneath, and this is where I'm more cautious. An agent product is mostly a thin wrapper around how well the base model can plan, recover from errors, and know when to stop. The gap between a demo that works on a scripted task and an agent you'd trust to run for twenty minutes unattended is almost entirely a model-capability gap. The leading domestic models have closed a lot of distance on reasoning and coding benchmarks, but long-horizon agentic reliability, the ability to not drift, not hallucinate a tool result, not confidently delete the wrong directory, is a different muscle. I've seen products that look polished but fall apart on step eight of a ten-step task. That's not a product problem, that's a post-training problem, and it can't be solved by a better UI.

The third layer is the one I actually find most interesting, which is who the product is for. OpenClaw's early adopters were developers who were comfortable giving a program broad permissions on their machine. In China, several teams are explicitly trying to skip that audience and go to ordinary knowledge workers or even consumers. That's a much harder design problem. You need safety rails that don't feel like handcuffs, and you need a cost structure that makes sense when the user isn't paying developer prices. A few teams have made real progress on that, especially on cost, because they're forced to be efficient. But I also think some of them are moving to the mass market before the underlying reliability justifies it, and the risk is that users have one bad experience, an agent books the wrong flight or sends the wrong message, and they don't come back.

So my overall assessment: strong on speed, strong on localization, decent on cost engineering, and still behind on the thing that actually determines whether these products survive, which is the model's judgment in open-ended situations. The teams that will win aren't the ones that copied the form fastest. They're the ones who treat the agent as a reason to go back and fix the model, rather than the other way around. I'd give it another twelve months before we know which of the current launches are products and which were announcements.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the excitement around these products from how useful they actually are. Giving an agent access to tools and letting it take several steps is a starting point. The harder question is whether it can complete a real task reliably, with a reasonable amount of supervision.

For teams in China, I’d look at how well the product fits the tools and workflows its users already have. Does it understand the task? Can it recover when something goes wrong? Does it know when to ask the user rather than keep going? And once you include the cost of checking and correcting its work, does it still save time?

So I wouldn’t judge a particular team without using its product. But broadly, I think this experimentation is valuable. What will distinguish these products is whether people keep trusting them with useful work after the initial curiosity wears off.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look less at how closely they resemble OpenClaw and more at whether they can reliably finish a real task. A polished demonstration is one thing; handling incomplete information, recovering from mistakes, and knowing when to ask the user is much harder.

For teams in China, adapting to local applications and workflows could be a real advantage. But if the products rely on similar underlying models, their capabilities may converge quickly. The differentiation will come from the whole system: tool integration, reliability, cost, and how much supervision the user needs.

So I’d welcome the experimentation, while being cautious about judging products from launch videos. The useful question is: after using it for a week, are you consistently handing work over to it, or are you still spending your time watching it and correcting it?
